item_description: Do They Know It's Christmas Single and Picture Disc
caption: 1 Band Aid ‘Do They Know It’s Christmas?’ Single and Picture Disc Following a BBC News report highlighting a famine in Ethiopia, Bob Geldof formed Band Aid - a super-group to record a charity single.  ‘Do They Know It’s Christmas?’ was co-written by Geldof and Midge Ure and the sleeve was designed by Sir Peter Blake. It was recorded on the 25th November 1984 and released just four days later in time for Christmas. The record went straight to number one, became the biggest selling record in chart history and raised over £8,000,000 for the relief effort.

After taking in the New York City club scene, they began to move towards more electronic and dance-based music. Their 1983 hit ‘Blue Monday’ is still the biggest-selling 12” single with more than one million copies sold. As Factory Records were not part of the BPI at the time, they were not presented with a Gold disc. Peter Saville, however, designed and commissioned this special award, based on the grinding wheel from the Movement LP, in recognition of its sales. By kind permission of New Order

caption: 6 Take That dolls and ephemera Boyzone fan club ephemera Spice Girls dolls and fan club ephemera The mid-1990s saw an increase in boy and girl bands targeted at the youth market. This attracted a range of merchandise on a scale unseen since the days of The Beatles in the 1960s. caption: 3 Hapshash and the Coloured Coat Pink Floyd at the UFO club poster Membership cards to the UFO club on Oxford Street 1967 In early 1967, Michael English and Nigel Waymouth joined forces to become poster designer Hapshash and the Coloured Coat. Their romantic, surreal illustrations, in part inspired by Art Nouveau, were commissioned by the underground UFO club and other music venues to advertise their events. Their silkscreen designs became a statement for the underground psychedelic community in the late 1960s – when people saw them, they knew exactly what to expect. By kind permission of Peter Golding

item_description: Bass guitar played by Bill Wyman
caption: 4 The Rolling Stones Bass guitar played by Bill Wyman Bill Wyman joined R&B band The Rolling Stones on bass guitar in 1962 as a replacement for Dick Taylor. He had previously been touring his own invention – the fretless bass - with his band The Cliftons on the London circuit. Impressing the group with his ability on guitar, the instrument itself and his vocals, Wyman sailed through The Rolling Stones audition. His ‘walking bass’ style of playing coupled with Charlie Watts’ drumming provided the distinctive pulsating sound behind a number of their hits. caption: 4 The Rolling Stones Bass guitar played by Bill Wyman Bill Wyman joined R&B band The Rolling Stones on bass guitar in 1962 as a replacement for Dick Taylor. He had previously been touring his own invention – the fretless bass - with his band The Cliftons on the London circuit. Impressing the group with his ability on guitar, the instrument itself and his vocals, Wyman sailed through The Rolling Stones audition. His ‘walking bass’ style of playing coupled with Charlie Watts’ drumming provided the distinctive pulsating sound behind a number of their hits. caption: 6 Queen ‘John Birch’ electric guitar and amp played by Brian May The first and probably most talked-about replica of Brian’s home made guitar, affectionately known as the Red Special, is simply called ‘the John Birch’. It was the main live backup to the Red Special during the late 1970s/early 1980s and famously appeared in Queen’s We Will Rock You and Spread Your Wings video shoots in 1977, before meeting an ignominious end at a show in New Jersey in 1982. “I wasn’t somebody who habitually smashed up his guitar or set alight to it, but there was one night, where I had broken a string and I had picked up a spare, which was the John Birch replica of my guitar, a pale brown-coloured Red Special, and the thing just didn’t cooperate – it wouldn’t play properly – I couldn’t get any sound out of it. It didn’t seem to be close to in tune and it sounded like a wet blanket to me; so in total frustration I lobbed it up in the air and had no idea where it would land.” Brian May In 2004, the guitar was rediscovered in bits and shipped back to Brian and repaired by Andrew Guyton Brian May would play the guitar with a Vox AC30 amplifier distorting at full power. This, combined with his unusual choice of a sixpence as a plectrum, helped to create his legendary guitar sound. By kind permission of Brian May
